title: Wisdom as practice
hook: the sixth: seeing things as they are, in every act

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth perfection: meditation, a steady mind built one sitting at a time, like the boy under the rose-apple tree. Did you find a patch of shade? Day one thousand four hundred four.

A coin, a bowl of rice, an hour of your time handed to someone who needs it. That is giving, the first perfection. But a gift can be given to show off. A precept can be kept with a sneer at the people who don't keep it. Patience can be gritted teeth, effort can be pride, and even a quiet mind can be one more thing to own. Something has to turn each of these into the real thing. In the Mahayana list, that something has a name, and it comes last, as the sixth. It is the one the other five lean on. Today, wisdom.
screen: `A GIFT CAN BE GIVEN TO SHOW OFF.` → `WHAT TURNS IT INTO THE REAL THING?` → `THE SIXTH.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is prajna, in Pali panna: wisdom, understanding, the mind that sees. In the old suttas, the phrase that goes with it is seeing things as they really are. And what is it to see things as they are? The Dhammapada puts it plainly in three short verses: all conditioned things pass away; all conditioned things are suffering, unable to fully satisfy; all things are without a self. When a person sees this with wisdom, the verses say, they grow weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. So wisdom here is not knowing lots of facts. It is seeing, right in the middle of a moment, that this too is changing, this too can't hold me up forever, and this too is not a solid me. Now the Mahayana turn. A whole family of sutras is named for this perfection: the perfection of wisdom, prajnaparamita. The short Heart Sutra belongs to it. Some of these texts compare the first five perfections to people who cannot see, and wisdom to the guide who leads them to the city. Without it, giving is just handing things over. With it, the giver sees there is no solid giver, no solid gift, no solid receiver to cling to, and gives freely anyway. That is why wisdom belongs in every act. Wisdom is not a sixth task added at the end of the list. It is the light the other five are done by: giving, keeping precepts, patience, effort and sitting, each one done with the eyes open.
screen: `PRAJNA: THE MIND THAT SEES.` · `CHANGING, UNSATISFYING, NOT SELF.` · `THE GUIDE WHO LEADS THE BLIND.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN EVERY ACT.`

segments.voice: Let's try seeing one thing clearly. Sit, and choose something small in front of you: a cup, your hand, the light on a wall. Look at it for a few breaths, as it is. Then notice: it is changing, even slowly. The light shifts. The hand warms or cools. Notice that it can't stay exactly like this. Then turn the same gentle look on a feeling you have right now, maybe restlessness, maybe ease. It too is changing. No need to think hard about it. Just see it, and let the seeing be enough. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom as practice. Prajna, the sixth perfection: seeing things as they are, the light every other perfection is done by. Today's word.
Your line: the sixth perfection. Once today, in the middle of something ordinary, washing up or waiting in line, say to yourself: this is changing. Then carry on. Day one thousand four hundred four.

screen: `DAY 1404 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MONTH OF MOON DAYS.`

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists count wisdom (prajna) as the sixth perfection and chant texts like the Heart Sutra from the perfection of wisdom sutras; in Theravada, wisdom (panna) is developed by seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in daily experience.

fork.setup: you give a gift, keep a precept, sit an hour. what turns each of these into a perfection, in the Mahayana view?
options: doing them with wisdom, seeing things as they are.
fork.reveal: some perfection of wisdom texts call the first five like people who can't see, and wisdom the guide that leads them.

original.note: Sanskrit prajna (Pali panna): wisdom, understanding; the sixth perfection, and the root of prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: wisdom is being clever or well read.
what it means: prajna, seeing things as they are, and doing every good act with that seeing.
what a scholar hears: the Dhammapada's verses on impermanence, suffering and not-self, and the perfection of wisdom sutras where wisdom guides the other perfections.

sources.ref: Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita (perfection of wisdom in 8,000 lines), the simile of the blind and the guide

notes: Dhammapada 277–279 paraphrased (Max Muller 1881 exists but wording not quoted for safety); 'three short verses' is the cited verse range. Confirm paraphrase, especially 'grow weary of suffering' and 'path to purity'.
The simile of the first five perfections as blind people and wisdom as the guide is attributed to the Astasahasrika (chapter 7 in some editions); framed as 'some of these texts'. Confirm the source.
'Seeing things as they really are' (yathabhuta) given as the phrase that goes with wisdom in the suttas; confirm.
The threefold emptiness of giver, gift and receiver is a standard Mahayana teaching on dana with prajna; confirm framing.
Pronunciation of prajna as PRUJ-nyah; regional pronunciations vary. Confirm.
